newsitem.title: INDIA: India's Tata Electric Cos. 96/97 net seen down.
newsitem.headline: India's Tata Electric Cos. 96/97 net seen down.

text.p: A fall in power offtake and a hike in regional power prices will short-circuit net profit at the Tata Electric Companies (TEC) in 1996/97 (April-March), analysts said on Wednesday.

TEC is a composite of three power generating companies, Tata Power Ltd, Andhra Valley Power Supply Company Ltd and Tata Hydro Electricity Power Supply Co Ltd, that supply power to India's financial capital.

The composite result of all three companies is due to be announced on June 26. The sales and profits are split in a ratio of five-to-three-to-two with the largest chunk to Tata Power and the smallest to Tata Hydro.

"TEC's unit sales of power are likely to drop about 9 percent. One of its largest buyers, Bombay Suburban Electric Supply Ltd (BSES) has also ventured into power generation," Rajesh Bharatkar, power analyst at Citicorp Securities and Investments Ltd, said.

He said that BSES has commissioned its 500 megawatt plant at Dahanu, and this had reduced its dependence on TEC by 40 percent. Historically, about 35 percent of TEC's power has been purchased by BSES, which distributed it to Bombay's suburbs.
Analysts said they expected TEC's net profit to fall to average 3.1 billion rupees in 1996/97 (April-March) from 4.45 billion rupees in 1995/96.
Sales were expected to fall too, analysts said, to an average 22.8 billion rupees in 1996/97 from 23.40 billion rupees in 1995/96.
Analysts said that the company's future growth prospects are not very positive, and that this would keep its profits flat.

"With BSES' purchases reduced, and no large power intensive industry coming up around Bombay, TEC will be forced to sell power to the Maharashtra State Electricity Board (MSEB)," said one analyst at a leading French investment house who did not want to be named.
He said that MSEB's per kilowatt hour realisation is 1.70 rupees as compared to 2.40 rupees from BSES.

He added TEC had hiked its power tariff along with that of MSEB, but had not been able to pass it on fully to BSES. "The company has not been able to benefit fully from this power tariff hike, and this will impact its profits."
Analysts said the company's lack of firm investment plans would keep its net profit flat for 1997/98 (April-March), though its revenues would rise.
They expected TEC's net to stay around the 3.2 billion rupee mark for 1997/98. Sales are expected to climb to an average 24.2 billion rupees.

"TEC will suffer until it can chart out a concrete investment plan. The status of its 450 megawatt project in Bhivpuri is unclear, as is that of its proposal to take over TISCO's plant near Jamshedpur," said an analyst at a leading Swiss bank.
He said that TEC had not been able to manage the state government well, though it was a well-managed and professionally-run company.
